messages.subject: random effects terms with procD.lm/lm.rrpp
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I have a quick question about using the error argument in anova() to incorporate nested random effects. I have some models that are structured exactly like the vignette, with a nested random factor (Y~ b.length+regime +regime:site), for which anova(error = c("Residuals", "regime:site", "Residuals")) seems to work great. But I also have a more complicated model, again using site:regime as a random factor nested within regime, but also including a species:regime interaction: (Y ~ species + regime + b.length + species:regime  + regime:site). In this case, because site is nested within regime, would the random "regime:site" term MS also be used for the denominator of the species:regime F-stat calculation (e.g., anova(error = c("Residuals", "regime:site", "Residuals", "regime:site", "Residuals"))?

I just want to make sure I was doing this the right way, since a colleague also ran this model as a traditional manova in SAS, and while we expected the results to differ between the two methods a bit, they were different enough that I wanted to double check that I am using this method properly.

Thanks very much
Grant

messages.body_plain:
Grant,

The error statement in anova.lm.rrpp can only use row names from the existing table, so as long as each term has a match to another term or the Residuals, a result is attainable.  The results are based on the random outcomes from RRPP.  Whether the result is what you expect from another program will depend on the process generating random outcomes and what the other program is doing for EMS calculations.

One really important reason for differences could be the type of SS used.  Also, the proc used for SAS might make a difference.  I would expect proc GLM to be more similar than proc Mixed, for example, as it uses LS calculations rather than REML estimation.

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Giorgio,

Could you please provide information about which geomorph and RRPP versions you are using?  This can be found with sessionInfo(), if you are not sure.

You have a redundancy problem with your variables, which could be one of two possible reasons.  One, you might have reduced your data set to use only a portion of it but left ghost factor levels in your factors.  (This commonly happens when an original variable has, for example, three factor levels but the data are reduced so that it is a binary variable, as you indicated.  The analysis still think a third level should be there if you do not explicitly update the factor.)  The second is that one variable is invariant with respect to the other variable, but you seek to establish an interaction in your model.

In a previous version of RRPP::lm.rrpp, which procD.lm and other function use, this would trigger an error but in the most recent update this should be fixed and avoided.

For everyone reading, if you seek help with errors, it is a good policy to include the following:

1. Package version used
2. Functions used or preferably, a portion of script showing how errors are produced.

This will make advice easier to provide without speculation and alert us to bugs we might need to fix.

Thanks,
Mike

Here is how one can do that with one line of code:

boas <- simplify2array(lapply(1:length(Y.gpa$Csize), function(j) Y.gpa$coords[,,j] * Y.gpa$Csize[j]))

Keep in mind that this — as Fred Bookstein suggested to do — is not the same as a Procrustes superimposition without scaling configurations to unit size.  It is scaling, then superimposition, then unscaling.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Paolo,

The code you sent seems to simply be the linear model table output.  However, I believe your question gets at whether one should interpret the separate versus common allometry analyses and plots. Part of that is evaluating the linear model table and making a determination as to the importance of the interaction term; as you did in your email. Then, once one makes that determination, the plot from the corresponding model is used.

Below is an example of this, adjusted from the help file for plotAllometry.  First I fit a linear model that includes the slope test (i.e., the interaction), and then the common allometry analysis and plot.  One could use this, plus biological judgement, as a guide.

Best,

Dean

##

data(plethodon)

Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land, print.progress = FALSE)    #GPA-alignment

gps <- interaction(plethodon$site, plethodon$species)

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, gps  = gps)

# Group Allometries

fit <- procD.lm(coords ~ Csize * gps, data=gdf, iter=999,

                print.progress = FALSE)

#NOTE INTERACTION DOES NOT PROVIDE EVIDENCE OF HETEROGENEOUS SLOPES

anova(fit)

# Predline: Plotting anyway for illustration

plotAllometry(fit, size = gdf$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "PredLine",

              pch = 19, col = gps)

# Common Allometry

# Group Allometries

fit.c <- procD.lm(coords ~ Csize + gps, data=gdf, iter=999,

                print.progress = FALSE)

anova(fit.c)

# Predline

plotAllometry(fit.c, size = gdf$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "PredLine",

              pch = 19, col = gps)

messages.body_plain:
Austin,

Because size is in such different units from aligned Procrustes coordinates, it will dominate any downstream analytics: PCA, MANOVA, etc. So having PC1 explaining 95% and that being size is to be expected (see the size-shape spaces in Mitteroecker et al. 2004).

As to your anova question and why your data do not show differences only in species 1, this is challenging to address without more information.  I would suggest some simple plots such as box plots and histograms to visually inspect the patterns among groups. That may assist you in discovering why your intuition about your data is not matching the analytics. Sample sizes may come into play here (and no, RRPP does not alleviate any issues regarding this).

As for the test statistic used in pairwise, ‘Dist’ is the correct one. “Var” is for comparing within-group variances = disparity.

Dean

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Testing for centroid size differences amongst different species

Hello!

So I am wrapping up some analyses looking at how including centroid size as a variable influences species discrimination. I ran my analyses with landmark data in two sets (One with just the landmark coordinates (Procrustes superimposed) and another with the superimposed coordinates and the log centroid size added as another variable.

I ran both data sets through PCA and to no surprise, species lacked clustering with shape exclusive analyses, but when size is added I saw separation between species 1 and all of the remaining species. The first PC explained ~95% of the variation, being centroid size. Based on this, and I know PCA is not a statistical test, I would assume that the only difference between the species I analyzed on the basis of centroid size alone would be between species one and the rest of the species. So in order to test this I ran a ProcD.lm with the following code to evaluate whether centroid size was significantly different amongst the species or not. I expected to find that species one was different from the remaining groups, but instead found that all species differed significantly in centroid size despite this pattern not showing up in the PCA?

#Run  ProcD.lm to test for sig differences in centroid sizes across groups

procA_size<-procD.lm(centroid~species,iter=1000,RRPP=TRUE)

summary(procA_size)

#Run pairwise comparison

PW_procA_size<-pairwise(procA_size,groups=species)

summary(PW_procA_size, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "dist")

I am working with fossil data, so the design is heavily unbalanced (species observations range anywhere from 2 - 190 specimens per species). I thought that this might be causing the discrepancy, but I am using the RRPP so it shouldn't be. I was also wondering if it could be the test.type I am using for the pairwise summary, should it be var instead of dist?

Sorry for the onslaught of questions, I am so thankful to have this group to refer to for questions!

Kindest regards,

Austin

I think I would advise (without knowing more about why you are trying to subset a gdf): subsetting your data before using geomorph.data.frame() if using for a linear model.

If one must subset a gdf, then you can do this by calling the gdf, the variable name, and then using the [] operators: gdf$var[#] or gdf$var[#,] depending on the dimensions of the original data. As far as I know one cannot subset all variables within a gdf at once using existing functions since the gdf is meant as direct input to lm.rrpp or related functions, but I am sure you could write custom code to subset all variables within a gdf using base operators or apply functions.

Best,

messages.body_plain:
As an additional note, if one has a data.frame object — which is a list that can be coerced into a matrix — the geomorph functions that use geomorph data frames can also use regular data frames, and those are easier to subset.

The reason for geomorph data frames is one cannot add things like class phylo trees to data frames and these cannot be subsetted easily.  Coordinates in 3d arrays cannot be added to regular data frames.  The geomorph data frame will check to make sure there are equal numbers of observation but is more like a standard list.  Subsetting of regular data frames is a convenience because rows can be removed.  In geomorph data frames, rows have less meaning.

Nonetheless, when functions like procD.lm come across regular data frames, they have no trouble to treat them the same as geomorph data frames.

Best,
Mike
